extracted.intended_audience: early-career researchers and other scientists asked to review manuscripts for ecology and evolution journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing peer review of scholarly manuscripts in ecology and evolution, covering whether to accept invitations, how to structure and write reviews, section-by-section evaluation criteria, ethical responsibilities, and post-review conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Three traditional forms of peer review are described: single-blind (authors do not know reviewers), double-blind (both authors and reviewers identities hidden), and open peer review (identities known to all parties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Box 1 gives examples of journals using each type. The booklet also describes other forms: cascading peer review (reviewer/editor comments forwarded to a second journal with author consent), third-party peer review services (e.g. Peerage of Science, Rubiq), post-publication peer review platforms (e.g. F1000Research) and preprint servers (arXiv, PeerJ PrePrints). Choose and be aware of the model used by the journal you are reviewing for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invitation — accept/decline decision checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: When invited to review ask: Does the subject area match my expertise? Do I have time to review within the timescale requested? Do I have any conflicts of interest? Do I actually want to review this article?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond straight away if declining. Many journals ask for reviews in 2–3 weeks; be realistic. If you accept, commit the time needed; if circumstances change inform the editorial office early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic principles of reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Core reviewer principles: confidentiality; objectivity and independence; attentiveness because your report influences editorial decisions; role to improve science via critical scrutiny; provide evidence for statements; use simple language; conduct reviews professionally, courteously, collegially and politely; never contact authors directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted advice includes 'Always treat the paper with the utmost confidentiality' and 'Be careful when writing a report to use simple language so that authors can understand your comments, even if English is not their first language.'

rubrics_metrics.name: How to get started as a reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reviewing, read the journal's aims and scope, the reviewer guidelines and the form the journal expects you to complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at which questions you are expected to answer. Read the article from start to finish before detailed appraisal to gain an overview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overview comments to include at report start
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening comments should address: clear and valid motivation for the study; whether the research question/hypothesis/prediction is clearly presented; whether the research follows logically from prior knowledge and is timely; whether the article is appropriately structured and clearly presented; a concise summary of the key message; whether the title reflects contents and is engaging; fit with the journal's scope; coverage of relevant literature; and overlap with previously published material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your answers to these questions should form the opening comments in your report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodical, section-by-section detailed review
rubrics_metrics.description: Appraise each section in turn (abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion/conclusion), providing evidence for statements whether positive or negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a methodical approach and provide section-specific comments rather than only general remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract/Summary checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the abstract concisely written? Does it provide a clear overview of the work? Does it contain the essential facts from the paper? Does the final point place the work in a broader context, highlighting its significance?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the abstract reflects the core findings and significance succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the introduction provide a clear, concise background? Does it enable understanding of the aims and hypotheses? Have authors elaborated the context sufficiently? Is the motivation adequately explained? Is there satisfactory citation of prior literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the introduction sets up the study and situates it within existing knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the methodology sound? Have procedures been sufficiently described? Is there enough detail for replication? Is it clear what was recorded and which units were used? Are statistical design and analyses appropriate? Have important details been left out? Where appropriate, has ethical approval been obtained?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for replicability, clarity of measurements and units, appropriateness of statistical methods, and presence of ethical approvals; request missing details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results presented so they are easy to interpret and understand? Have results for all questions been provided? Are the data of sufficient quality and quantity? Are figures and tables appropriate? Have the correct units been used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check completeness and clarity; ensure figures/tables convey necessary information without ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion and conclusions checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the authors answered their research questions/hypotheses? Are the conclusions justified by the results? Has the significance of the study been fully explained? By how much has this study advanced current understanding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether interpretations are supported and whether the claimed contribution is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary points for writing the review (Box 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key principles: Be objective; include details of what is good and highlight problems; look for novelty and importance; recognize that no study is perfect; be constructive; be thorough and thoughtful; evaluate both the quality of ideas and experimental details/results; be specific and factually accurate; recognize opinion versus fact; be civil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as a touchstone to ensure reviews are balanced, constructive and useful to editors and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-review responsibilities and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible agree to review revisions/resubmissions you previously reviewed to provide consistency. Do not include anything that appears to be a decision about the paper in comments to authors (decisions are made by editors). Expect the journal to copy other reviewers' comments to you. The journal will not reveal your identity without permission; if identity is revealed and a dispute arises, advise authors to contact the editorial office rather than contacting them directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be available for follow-up and maintain confidentiality; understand boundaries between reviewer comments and editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can request that a journal reconsider a rejection. Appeals are often dealt with by the editor and associate editor; in rare cases technical details may lead the editor to approach reviewers for further comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are approached about an appeal, provide additional technical insight if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: In traditional peer review you are bound to confidentiality: do not take ideas or data from articles you review and pass them off as your own or disclose data before publication. It is acceptable to ask a colleague for advice as long as authors' names are not revealed and unnecessary details remain confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain strict confidentiality; seek permission before involving others and avoid naming authors when consulting colleagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias awareness and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be sensitive to biases that may affect judgement including gender bias, geographical bias, seniority bias and confirmation bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of these possible biases and check whether your opinion may have been influenced by them; base your opinion solely on the presented work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of research ethics problems reviewers should spot
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions/examples given: fabricated data (made up), falsified data (measurements unjustifiably altered), stealing data (using someone else's data without consent), animal welfare practice breaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should report concerns about unethical practice to the editorial office; journals have procedures to investigate while protecting reviewer anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication ethics — duplicate/multiple submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple submission is submitting an article concurrently to multiple journals or submitting overlapping material; duplicate publication is publishing the same or highly similar material in more than one journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alert editors if you suspect duplicate submission or publication; these are breaches of publishing ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship should be granted to those who substantially contributed. Unjustified authorship (gift/honorary/guest) assigns authorship to those who did not make substantial contributions. Ghost authorship omits those who have contributed substantially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise authorship concerns with the editorial office rather than confronting authors directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest (COI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of interest that prevent a reviewer from impartially evaluating someone else’s work should be declared and may prohibit reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have a COI, decline or disclose it to the editorial office; do not let COIs influence review content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passing a review to a student / mentoring junior reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: You may decline and suggest a student as an alternative, or use the invitation as a mentoring opportunity by having a student draft the review under your supervision. You must inform the journal in advance and seek consent; include the student's name so they get credit. If the student does most of the work, the review could be submitted under their name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully check any student-prepared review before submission and ensure appropriate credit is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing with a supervisor
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing with your supervisor is a way to practice reviewing under supervision. Discussing the article helps you learn important points and develop your own reviewing ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use supervised reviews as training but ensure the journal is informed if others contribute to the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asking colleagues for advice on a review
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to ask a colleague for advice on particular aspects (e.g. statistics) provided authors' names are not revealed and unnecessary article details remain confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep confidentiality and seek editorial permission if in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data archiving and the reviewer's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals recommend or mandate data archiving in public repositories; depositing data is usually required after acceptance. Reviewers are not normally expected to review archived data unless the journal explicitly states data review is part of the task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If archived data are available you may inspect them, but check journal policy (e.g. Molecular Ecology required data review at time of writing). Embargo periods are possible for data underlying other articles in preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting information and supplementary files
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporting information or supplementary files are usually provided at submission but most journals do not expect them to be reviewed. These files are not part of the version of record but are usually posted online with the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may consult supplementary files for further understanding or recommend moving material between main article and supporting information; request additional supporting information if needed to support conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access versus subscription journal reviewing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Some open access journals (e.g. PLOS ONE) only require reviewers to comment on scientific and ethical integrity and clarity of presentation, not importance or novelty; other OA journals (PLOS Biology, eLife) are highly selective and ask reviewers to judge importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarise yourself with the specific journal guidelines and apply appropriate standards depending on the journal's criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting standards to journal aims and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: While judging the science is central, reviewers should keep in mind a journal's aims and scope and the quality of articles expected; what is acceptable for one journal (e.g. case studies) may not be for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether and why you would expect the article to appear in the particular journal in your confidential comments to the editor and support your opinion with reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to spend on a review
rubrics_metrics.description: Time depends on familiarity with the topic, experience, clarity of the article, difficulty, and length/type of article. A survey found review quality increased with time spent up to 3 hours but not beyond; a sensible guideline is to set aside 3–5 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to spend 3–5 hours; do not spend excessive time correcting hopelessly poor submissions but indicate grave and consistent problems if present.

rubrics_metrics.name: When not to invest excessive time on very poor manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: If an article is of insufficient quality to justify detailed review and you notice grave and consistent problems throughout, indicate this in your comments but do not feel obliged to spend significant time correcting errors the authors could not or did not care to correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be more lenient with inexperienced authors or those for whom English is not a first language; point out major issues succinctly rather than copyediting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing confidential comments to editor versus comments to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential comments to editors should not be significantly different in overall message from comments to authors; however, statements about whether an article should be published should only be made in confidential comments to the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep consistency between messages while reserving publication recommendations for the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor decision factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors make final decisions guided by: aims and scope of the journal; associate editor recommendation; reviewer comments; other articles recently published in the journal; journal priorities; and journal page budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that the editor balances multiple considerations beyond the reviewers' recommendations; well-argued reviews help editors in cases of conflicting advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate editor (handling editor) responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate editors make an initial expert assessment; select appropriate reviewers; scrutinize reviewers' comments; provide their own assessment with suggestions and guidance on the importance of reviewer comments; judge merits of publishing in the targeted journal; make a recommendation to the editor; and support editors in promoting the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their role bridges reviewers and the editor; reviewers should be aware their assessment will be weighed alongside the associate editor's judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibilities (explicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are to provide a detailed, objective report on the merits of an article; identify flaws in design, analysis and interpretation; highlight ethical concerns; comment on appropriateness of cited literature; and offer their view on suitability for publication in the targeted journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on objective, evidence-based critique and on issues that materially affect the validity of the research and its presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial office duties relevant to reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial office checks that files are complete and adhere to author guidelines; provides a central contact; gives essential feedback to parties; provides publishing advice to editors; handles correspondence including some decision letters; and prepares copy in house-style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the editorial office as the contact point for logistical questions, reporting ethical concerns, and communicating availability or conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should peer review? (qualifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should be carried out by those suitably qualified: expertise can come from many years' academic/research experience, in-depth PhD study in a specific area, or practical field experience. Editors often select reviewers who have recently published on a related subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept review invitations only when you have the appropriate expertise to judge the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cascading and alternative pre-submission feedback options
rubrics_metrics.description: Cascading peer review: journals refer declined articles to another journal and forward reviewer/editor comments with author consent. Third-party review services can arrange independent peer review prior to journal submission. Preprint servers allow early posting for peer feedback but are not formal peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and reviewers should be aware of these models; reviewers may encounter manuscripts previously reviewed elsewhere or on preprint servers.
